questions.q: Why does trial division only need to test divisors up to √n?
o: Because n / 2 would be too slow
If n = a × b with a ≤ b, then a ≤ √n
questions.h: Divisors come in pairs d and n / d.
questions.e: If both factors were above √n, their product would be above n. So any factorisation has one factor at most √n, and finding none up to √n means n is prime.

questions.q: In the sieve, why does the inner loop start at j = i * i?
o: Because i * i is always prime
Smaller multiples of i were already crossed out by smaller primes
questions.h: Take i = 5. Who already crossed out 10, 15 and 20?
questions.e: Any multiple k × i with k < i has a prime factor smaller than i, so it was crossed out earlier. The first new one is i × i.

questions.q: This function should return true if n is prime, testing divisors only up to √n. Which condition goes in the blank?
questions.h: Test it on n = 9 and n = 4.
questions.e: i * i <= n checks every i up to √n. With i * i < n, 9 and 25 would count as prime; with i < n / 2, n = 4 never enters the loop and is called prime.

questions.q: This sieve should leave every prime up to n marked true and everything else false. Which loop header goes in the blank?
o: int j = i * i; j <= n; j += i
int j = 2; j <= n; j *= i
int j = i; j <= n; j += i
int j = i * i; j < n; j++
questions.h: Cross out the multiples of i, but never i itself.
questions.e: Start at i * i and step by i. Starting at i crosses out the prime itself; j++ crosses out non-multiples; j < n skips n.

questions.q: This code prints all divisors of n by finding them in pairs (d and n / d). Which condition stops a divisor from being printed twice?
questions.h: For n = 36, what happens at d = 6?
questions.e: When d × d = n, the pair is (6, 6), so the partner must not be printed again. Print n / d only when it differs from d.

questions.q: This function should return true only for prime numbers. For n = 1 it returns true, but 1 is not prime. What is missing?
o: if (n < 2) return false; at the start
questions.h: Does the loop run at all for n = 1?
questions.e: For n = 0 and 1 the loop never runs, so the function falls through to return true. Neither is prime, so reject n < 2 first.

questions.q: This sieve should leave every prime up to n marked true. For n = 30 only 7 11 13 17 19 23 29 stay marked: 2, 3 and 5 are lost. What is the fix?
questions.drive:
vector<bool> p = sieve(30);
for (int i = 0; i <= 30; i++) if (p[i]) cout << i << " ";
o: Start j at i * i (or 2 * i), not at i
Use j++ instead of j += i
questions.h: What is the first value of j, and what does it cross out?
questions.e: j = i crosses out i itself, so every prime up to √30 (2, 3, 5) is lost. Start at i * i.

questions.q: This function should count the divisors of n. For n = 36 it returns 10, but 36 has 9 divisors (1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36). What is the fix?
o: Add 1 instead of 2 when d == n / d
questions.h: Which divisor pair of 36 is the same number twice?
questions.e: 6 × 6 = 36 is counted as two divisors. Use c += (d == n / d) ? 1 : 2;

questions.q: A prime check uses for (int i = 2; i * i <= n; i++) with int i. What goes wrong for n = 2147483647, the largest int?
o: i * i overflows int once i passes 46340
n % i is undefined for large n
questions.e: 46341² is larger than INT_MAX, so i * i overflows before the loop can stop. Write (long long)i * i <= n or i <= n / i.

questions.q: How many divisors does 1 have, and is 1 prime?
questions.h: A prime has exactly two different divisors.
questions.e: 1 has only itself as a divisor. A prime needs exactly two (1 and itself), so 1 is not prime. Checks must handle 0, 1 and 2 correctly.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of the sieve up to n?
questions.h: Each prime p crosses out about n / p numbers.
questions.e: n/2 + n/3 + n/5 + … (over primes) is about n log log n, which is nearly linear. For n = 10^7 it runs in well under a second.

questions.q: How much memory does a sieve up to n = 10^7 need?
questions.h: The sieve keeps one flag per number.
questions.e: One flag per number from 0 to n, so O(n). vector<bool> stores them as bits, about 1.25 MB for 10^7.

questions.q: Answer 10^5 queries “is x prime?” with x ≤ 10^6. What is the best approach?
o: Sieve once up to 10^6, then answer each query in O(1)
Count the divisors of x up to x for every query
Run a new sieve for every query
Trial division up to x for every query
questions.h: Many queries on the same small range: do the work once.
questions.e: One sieve costs about 10^6 · log log 10^6 steps, and then every query is an array lookup. Checking up to x per query would be 10^5 × 10^6 = 10^11 steps.
